Military force can be an instrument of strategy. It cannot substitute for one.

virals.hook:
Israel’s Iran Strategy: Not a Nuclear Deal, but Strategic Capitulation 

Israel’s strategy toward Iran is actually quite straightforward: eliminate Iran’s strategic capabilities, initially its nuclear program and now its ballistic missile arsenal as well. This can be achieved, in Israel’s view, through toppling the regime, military pressure that forces Tehran to surrender its strategic assets, or by weakening Iran so dramatically that it becomes a failed state, unable to generate the resources needed to rebuild its military capabilities.

In other words, Netanyahu is not interested in a nuclear agreement that prevents Iran from developing nuclear weapons while allowing the Islamic Republic to survive and potentially strengthen itself. His objective goes far beyond the nuclear issue. It is about forcing Iran to abandon the capabilities that Israel considers threatening. The underlying assumption is simple: if military force fails to achieve the desired outcome, even greater force might succeed.

I suspect Netanyahu understands perfectly well that someone like Reza Pahlavi is unlikely to return to Tehran and take power. But regime change is not necessarily the only acceptable outcome for him, but Dramatically weakening the Islamic Republic to the point where its leadership must choose between rebuilding its military capabilities and ensuring its own survival would also serve Israel’s strategic objectives.

This is why I believe the discussion about the Iranian people, democracy, and political transition largely misses the point. It has been to deprive Iran of its strategic capabilities, by force if necessary. 

And this brings us to the fundamental difference between Netanyahu’s approach and a diplomatic strategy focused on nuclear nonproliferation. A nuclear agreement, even a strong and verifiable one that prevents Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, would not necessarily satisfy Netanyahu because it would leave the Islamic Republic in power, with the possibility of rebuilding its broader military strength.

The real question, therefore, is not whether Iran can be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons through diplomacy. It is whether Israel, under Netanyahu, is prepared to accept an agreement that addresses the nuclear threat without fundamentally weakening the Iranian regime. I believe the answer is no.

And that is precisely why the prospects for a diplomatic solution remain so limited in Israel view. The real question is if a new government will adopt the same approach.
.#Iran
#IranWar

outsiders.name: Danny (Dennis) Citrinowicz ,داني سيترينوفيتش
outsiders.hook:
Reasons for Both Optimism and Pessimism

On the one hand, Eizenkot is right about one thing: Israel cannot bring down the Islamic Republic through airpower alone, even with full American military support.

On the other hand, the Iranian regime has no intention of abandoning its nuclear and conventional military capabilities or its relationships with the so-called Axis of Resistance. As long as the regime survives, these will remain central pillars of its national security strategy.

This leaves Israel and the United States facing a fundamental strategic dilemma. Military operations may damage Iranian capabilities, but they cannot eliminate them. And even another large-scale military campaign is unlikely to produce the political transformation in Tehran that some in Washington and Jerusalem continue to envision.

The conclusion should be obvious: Israel's next government must fundamentally reassess its strategy toward Iran. The current approach is neither realistic nor sustainable. Worse, it risks trapping Israel, and potentially the United States, in an endless cycle of military confrontations without achieving a decisive strategic outcome.

Before Washington and Jerusalem contemplate another attack, they should answer a basic question: What exactly is the strategic objective, and how would another war achieve what the previous two failed to accomplish?

After two military campaigns, Iran's military capabilities have not been eliminated, and the Islamic Republic remains in power.

At some point, policymakers must confront an uncomfortable question: Is there really a military solution to the Iranian challenge, or are we simply preparing for another war that will leave us confronting the same fundamental threats, at an even higher cost?

Military force can be an instrument of strategy. It cannot substitute for one.

outsiders.name: Danny (Dennis) Citrinowicz ,داني سيترينوفيتش
outsiders.hook:
Israel’s Iran Strategy: Not a Nuclear Deal, but Strategic Capitulation 

Israel’s strategy toward Iran is actually quite straightforward: eliminate Iran’s strategic capabilities, initially its nuclear program and now its ballistic missile arsenal as well. This can be achieved, in Israel’s view, through toppling the regime, military pressure that forces Tehran to surrender its strategic assets, or by weakening Iran so dramatically that it becomes a failed state, unable to generate the resources needed to rebuild its military capabilities.

In other words, Netanyahu is not interested in a nuclear agreement that prevents Iran from developing nuclear weapons while allowing the Islamic Republic to survive and potentially strengthen itself. His objective goes far beyond the nuclear issue. It is about forcing Iran to abandon the capabilities that Israel considers threatening. The underlying assumption is simple: if military force fails to achieve the desired outcome, even greater force might succeed.

I suspect Netanyahu understands perfectly well that someone like Reza Pahlavi is unlikely to return to Tehran and take power. But regime change is not necessarily the only acceptable outcome for him, but Dramatically weakening the Islamic Republic to the point where its leadership must choose between rebuilding its military capabilities and ensuring its own survival would also serve Israel’s strategic objectives.

This is why I believe the discussion about the Iranian people, democracy, and political transition largely misses the point. It has been to deprive Iran of its strategic capabilities, by force if necessary. 

And this brings us to the fundamental difference between Netanyahu’s approach and a diplomatic strategy focused on nuclear nonproliferation. A nuclear agreement, even a strong and verifiable one that prevents Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, would not necessarily satisfy Netanyahu because it would leave the Islamic Republic in power, with the possibility of rebuilding its broader military strength.

The real question, therefore, is not whether Iran can be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons through diplomacy. It is whether Israel, under Netanyahu, is prepared to accept an agreement that addresses the nuclear threat without fundamentally weakening the Iranian regime. I believe the answer is no.

And that is precisely why the prospects for a diplomatic solution remain so limited in Israel view. The real question is if a new government will adopt the same approach.
.#Iran
#IranWar

outsiders.name: Iran International English
outsiders.hook:
Retaliation against the US and Israel for the killing of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei is certain, an Iranian lawmaker said on Wednesday, warning those responsible would face “severe punishment.”

“We will certainly not let the blood of our martyred leader go unavenged. Revenge against the US and Israel is certain,” Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee.

Rezaei also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the other side accepted and fully implemented Iran’s conditions.

“Reopening the Strait of Hormuz requires the other side to accept all of the Islamic Republic of Iran’s conditions,” he said.

He made the remarks in response to questions about possible renewed fighting and reports of potential attacks on US officials.
